name: Fourth Branchial Cleft Anomaly

diagnosticCriteria.formalCriteriaName: Clinical and Radiological Diagnostic Criteria for Fourth Branchial Cleft Anomaly

criteria.description: Recurrent neck swelling or abscess localized to the lower anterior neck or thyroid region
Identification of an internal sinus or fistula opening in the pyriform sinus by endoscopy
Imaging evidence (CT, MRI, or barium swallow) demonstrating a tract originating from the pyriform sinus extending to the neck
Histological confirmation of branchial cleft cyst or fistula lined by respiratory epithelium

diagnosticCriteria.minimumForDiagnosis: Presence of recurrent neck swelling or abscess with identification of a pyriform sinus fistula by endoscopy or imaging
diagnosticCriteria.notes: Diagnosis is often delayed due to rarity and similarity to other neck masses or infections.

pathognomonic.notes: Visible or endoscopically identified internal opening

searchTerms: repeated abscesses in lower front neck
neck infections recurring in lower anterior area
chronic neck abscess in front lower neck

pathognomonic.symptomName: Cervical cystic mass in the lower neck
searchTerms: cystic neck mass in cervical area
redness and pain in neck skin
thyroid involvement with swelling or pain

rare.symptomName: Airway obstruction due to mass effect
searchTerms: breathing difficulty due to neck swelling
airway obstruction caused by mass effect

rare.symptomName: Fistula tract extending into the mediastinum
searchTerms: neck fistula spreading into chest area

rare.symptomName: Sepsis secondary to deep neck infection
searchTerms: blood infection from deep neck infection
systemic infection secondary to neck infection

laboratory: Elevated inflammatory markers (e.g., ESR, CRP) during infection
imaging: CT or MRI showing cystic lesion or fistulous tract from pyriform sinus to neck
Barium swallow demonstrating contrast leakage into fistula tract
other: Endoscopic visualization of pyriform sinus fistula opening
Histopathology showing respiratory epithelium lining cyst or fistula

distinguishingFeatures: Fistula tract originates from the lower pyriform sinus apex but courses differently
Typically located higher in the neck compared to fourth branchial anomalies
Midline neck mass rather than lateral
No fistulous tract to pyriform sinus
Moves with swallowing or tongue protrusion
Usually resolves with antibiotics without recurrence

redFlags: Recurrent neck abscesses despite antibiotic therapy
Sepsis or systemic infection from deep neck space involvement
